exam: A 22‑year‑old with two second‑trimester losses presents at 16 weeks; what is the next investigation — transvaginal cervical length measurement to assess competence.
During a routine scan a cervix measures 18 mm; what management is indicated — offer prophylactic cerclage before 24 weeks if no infection.
A woman at 22 weeks has painless dilation to 2 cm with intact membranes; what is the immediate step — place a McDonald cerclage if no contraindications.
How does cervical insufficiency differ from preterm labor — insufficiency lacks painful contractions and shows painless dilation.
Why is progesterone preferred over tocolytics in a short cervix without contractions — it improves cervical integrity without maternal side‑effects of tocolytics.
A patient with active genital infection is considered for cerclage; what should you do — treat infection first; cerclage is contraindicated until cleared.
What are the risks of leaving a short cervix untreated — increased chance of mid‑trimester loss and preterm birth.
If ultrasound is unavailable, how can you monitor cervical change — perform careful serial digital examinations with sterile technique.
ai.title: Cervical Insufficiency
ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: Cervical insufficiency is painless cervical dilatation in the second trimester leading to recurrent mid‑trimester loss. Diagnosis relies on history, ultrasound, and exclusion of infection or trauma.

b: Painless cervical dilation without uterine contractions
History of prior second‑trimester loss or preterm birth
Often associated with prior cervical surgery or congenital anomalies
sections.p: A weak cervical stroma cannot maintain closure under the weight of the growing pregnancy, usually between 14–28 weeks. It is a diagnosis of exclusion.

b: Stage I: Cervical length <25 mm on transvaginal ultrasound
Stage II: Dilatation 1–3 cm, membranes intact
Stage III: Dilatation >3 cm or prolapsed membranes
sections.p: Cervical insufficiency is a structural problem (cervical competence) rather than a functional uterine cause. It is categorized by severity of dilation and membrane status.

b: Most common cause of second‑trimester loss in low‑resource settings
Associated with prior cone biopsy, LEEP, uterine anomalies, connective‑tissue disorders
sections.p: Recurrent mid‑trimester loss threatens maternal mental health and future fertility. Early detection allows prophylactic cerclage or progesterone therapy, reducing preterm birth.

t.b: Is the cervix short? <25 mm predicts insufficiency; if unavailable, perform digital exam with caution
Are membranes visualised or bulging? Presence supports diagnosis

t.a: Maternal infection screen (urine culture, STI panel)
t.b: Rule out infection as alternative cause of preterm loss
Identify treatable infections that may mimic or coexist

b: Cerclage (McDonald) before 24 weeks for women with prior loss and short cervix
Progesterone (vaginal micronized) for women with short cervix who cannot have cerclage
Avoid uterine irritants (e.g., NSAIDs, heavy lifting) and treat infections promptly
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, then provide mechanical or hormonal support. Monitor with serial ultrasounds.

b: Preterm labor: painful contractions, cervical effacement
PPROM: pooling of fluid, positive nitrazine or ferning
sections.p: Distinguish cervical insufficiency from preterm labor, which features uterine contractions and cervical change, and from premature rupture of membranes, which has fluid leakage.

b: Transient shortening after intercourse may normalize; repeat scan in 1 week
sections.p: A normal cervical length does not completely exclude insufficiency if rapid dilation occurs later; serial exams are essential.

b: Always ask about prior cervical procedures
Explain why cerclage is contraindicated with active infection
State the next step if membranes are prolapsed at 20 weeks
sections.p: Examiners test integration of history, imaging, and management choices.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden painless cervical dilation with bulging membranes
Vaginal bleeding or fluid loss at any gestational age
Signs of infection (fever, foul discharge) in a pregnant woman
